title: Counting animals after dark
bodyMd:
A team surveying a fictional nocturnal mammal once estimated abundance by counting sightings along forest paths. When thermal cameras became available, recorded sightings increased sharply. The simplest interpretation was population growth. Yet the cameras had changed not only how many animals could be seen but which animals were likely to be seen. Individuals remaining behind foliage or far from the path had previously been missed more often than those crossing open ground. A count can seem especially authoritative when it comes from a device that produces stored images rather than a human observer's notebook. Images permit later checking of what was recorded, which is a real advantage. They do not show every animal that failed to enter the device's field of detection. Verifying the identity of observed individuals and estimating the probability of observing individuals are separate tasks. A clearer record of encounters therefore need not provide a complete account of the population from which those encounters were selected.

To connect the two series, the researchers operated visual surveys and cameras together for a season. The comparison did not yield one stable multiplier. On dry nights the two methods produced similar rankings of sites, but after rain their relationship changed. Wet foliage altered the camera view, while animals also changed where they moved. A correction based only on the average difference between devices would therefore hide meaningful variation in detectability.

This problem is sometimes treated as an unfortunate technical nuisance, external to the ecological question. It is better understood as part of that question. The behavior that makes an animal detectable can itself respond to habitat, weather, and disturbance. Counting methods do not merely add random noise to an otherwise complete view; they select encounters through a biological process.

The team consequently separated two aims. For monitoring change within a site under comparable conditions, a consistent method could still provide useful evidence. For comparing absolute abundance across different habitats, they needed an explicit account of how detection varied. More sophisticated equipment did not remove the need for that account. It made previously hidden differences visible and thus required a more careful definition of what the count represented.
